content: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy cloud-security rival Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion, the companies announced on Monday, in what would be the largest cybersecurity acquisition ever recorded. The deal unites two of the industry's biggest names at a moment when artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster, cheaper and harder to stop. Under the terms announced on Monday, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each Zscaler share they own. Based on CrowdStrike's closing share price on Friday, that values Zscaler at about $260.41 a share, a premium of roughly 34 percent to its last close, according to Reuters. Zscaler shares had ended Friday's trading at $194.82, giving the company a market value of about $31.8 billion. The boards of both companies have unanimously approved the agreement, which is subject to shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028. If completed, the transaction would eclipse Alphabet's $32 billion acquisition of the cloud-security firm Wiz in 2025, previously the biggest deal in the sector's history. It also caps a blockbuster year for mergers and acquisitions, and it is the eighth acquisition announced by CrowdStrike since August of last year, and its third this month alone. The logic of the deal, as presented by both companies, is breadth. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform protects computers, servers and other devices — the endpoint — while Zscaler's technology secures the way employees connect to applications and data, through its zero-trust network access tools. Brought together, the combined company would offer corporate and government customers a single platform covering both, at a time when those customers are trying to cut the number of security vendors they manage. The combined business is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, including roughly $3.9 billion from Zscaler, and the companies say the deal expands their addressable market by more than $185 billion by 2029, in part by letting CrowdStrike sell its products to Zscaler's roughly 8,000 customers. George Kurtz, CrowdStrike's chief executive, will lead the combined company. Jay Chaudhry, Zscaler's founder, chairman and chief executive, will stay on to run the Zscaler business and will join CrowdStrike's board. Chaudhry, together with affiliated entities holding about 34 percent of Zscaler's outstanding shares, has signed voting agreements supporting the transaction. Once the deal closes, existing CrowdStrike shareholders are expected to own about 84 percent of the combined company, with Zscaler shareholders holding the rest. The agreement carries a $1.4 billion breakup fee payable by Zscaler if it walks away under certain circumstances, including to accept a rival offer. The deal will now face the scrutiny that comes with its size. Regulators in the United States will review a combination of two of the largest pure-play cybersecurity vendors, and the companies will have to argue that the market they operate in remains fragmented and fiercely competitive, with large rivals such as Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft, as well as hundreds of smaller firms, still competing for the same budgets. That argument has worked for big technology deals before, but the scale of this one — nearly $44 billion in a sector where the previous record was $32 billion — means the review is unlikely to be quick or quiet. For customers, the promise is simplicity: one vendor, one platform, one bill. The risk, which analysts have already begun to raise, is the opposite — that a combined giant with pricing power over both endpoint and network security could eventually charge more, and that integrating two large, distinct product lines could distract both companies while rivals keep shipping. CrowdStrike's recent record gives both sides something to point to: its acquisition pace has been rapid, but the company has also had to manage the fallout of the global IT outage in 2024, which damaged trust with some customers and is still cited by competitors. The timing of the announcement was, in one sense, unfortunate for both companies. It landed on one of the most extraordinary days in recent market history, the day Jensen Huang returned as chief executive of Nvidia after an 11-day absence, a story that dominated Wall Street's attention. As Barron's put it, on any other Monday a $44 billion cybersecurity deal would have been the talk of the market. Instead it was, briefly, the second-biggest story of the day. There is also a less-noticed dimension to the deal: both companies maintain major research and development centres in Israel, and the combined business will be one of the largest employers in the country's cybersecurity sector. The market's first verdict will come in the coming days, in the movement of both companies' shares and in the reaction of customers and rivals. The longer verdict — whether two giants can be stitched into one platform without losing the speed that made each of them successful — will take years, and will be judged not by the size of the price tag but by whether the combined company can stop the attacks that keep getting through. title: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $44 billion deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition ever
